title: Song of Solomon 3:1–5
context: The WEB prints no speaker labels in chapter 3, and interpreters commonly read 3:1–5 as the Beloved continuing to speak. She tells of seeking by night the one whom her soul loves, searching the city streets and squares, asking the watchmen, and at last finding him and holding him fast. Some interpreters take the scene as a dream or a poetic picture of longing, and others as a narrated event; the text does not settle the matter. A similar night scene appears in 5:2–8, with a different outcome. The section closes with the same refrain as 2:7, urging the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken love until it so desires. Literal readers commonly see the ache of separation and the joy of reunion in committed love; figurative readers commonly hear the soul seeking God and finding him (compare Isaiah 26:9; Jeremiah 29:13). Readers in both Arminian and Reformed traditions commonly hold both readings, and they commonly read the refrain as counsel to patience.

verses.text: By night on my bed, I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I didn’t find him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved seeking by night the one whom her soul loves, and not finding him. Love feels the pain of absence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see honest longing in separation. Figurative readers commonly hear the soul seeking God in seasons when he seems distant (compare Isaiah 26:9).

verses.text: I will get up now, and go about the city; in the streets and in the squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I didn’t find him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved rising to search the city streets and squares. Love takes action and goes out to seek the beloved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see earnest seeking that does not give up. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of wholehearted desire.

verses.text: The watchmen who go about the city found me; “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the watchmen finding the Beloved and her asking whether they have seen him. She seeks help in her search.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the watchmen as part of the scene rather than the goal of the search. Some figurative readers apply the image to those who keep watch over God’s people.

verses.text: I had scarcely passed from them, when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother’s house, into the room of her who conceived me.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved finding the one whom her soul loves and holding him fast. Seeking ends in joyful reunion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the joy of finding after long searching. Figurative readers commonly hear God’s promise that those who seek him will find him (compare Jeremiah 29:13; Proverbs 8:17).

verses.text: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, or by the hinds of the field, that you not stir up nor awaken love, until it so desires.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the refrain repeated, urging the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken love until it so desires. Patience guards love.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same counsel as in 2:7. Readers in both traditions commonly read the refrain as shared ground about restraint and waiting for love’s proper time.
